name: Dersimelagon

card.summary: MT-7117, an investigational oral MC1R agonist that darkens skin pigment to protect people with light-sensitivity disorders; it is not a tanning product and has no looks-related trials.
card.note: Investigational drug studied for erythropoietic protoporphyria and systemic sclerosis; not approved as of the sources reviewed, and not studied for cosmetic tanning.

quick.overview:
Dersimelagon (MT-7117) is an experimental pill that switches on the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R), the receptor that drives skin pigment production. It is being developed for rare light-sensitivity diseases, mainly erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) and X-linked protoporphyria (XLP), and for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis [2][3][7].

It is covered here because it is a pigment-related compound, a non-peptide cousin of injectable tanning peptides. No study has looked at it as a cosmetic tan or for appearance in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: It is an orally available, non-peptide, selective MC1R agonist that increases skin eumelanin, the dark pigment [6][8]. In EPP and XLP, more pigment is intended to reduce painful reactions to visible light [6]. MC1R activation also has anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects in laboratory models, which is why it was studied in systemic sclerosis [9].
quick.risks: Its safety and efficacy are described by reviewers as needing further characterization [2]. Because it targets the pigment pathway, skin darkening is an expected pharmacological effect. It is investigational, so it has no consumer product or legal cosmetic status.

lead: Dersimelagon (formerly MT-7117; developed as dersimelagon phosphoric acid) is an investigational, orally administered, nonpeptide small-molecule selective agonist of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) [8][9][10]. Activation of MC1R drives melanogenesis in pigment cells and also has anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects [10].

It has been studied for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) and X-linked protoporphyria (XLP), rare disorders in which accumulating protoporphyrin causes painful phototoxic reactions to visible light, and for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis [3][7][8]. The only approved treatment for EPP at the time of recent reviews is afamelanotide, a peptide MC1R agonist given as a subcutaneous implant [2][10].
The compound is of interest to the wiki's pigment category rather than as a cosmetic product. No published study has tested it for tanning or appearance in healthy people, and it is not marketed.
infobox: EPP, XLP, diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis [8]

paras: Patients with protoporphyria. A randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine enrolled 102 patients (93 with EPP and 9 with XLP) aged 18 to 75, who received placebo or dersimelagon at 100 mg or 300 mg once daily for 16 weeks; the primary endpoint was the change in time to first prodromal symptom on sunlight exposure, recorded in an electronic diary [6]. Later phase 3 studies in EPP and XLP are registered, including a 184-participant efficacy and safety trial, a 286-participant extension, and another phase 3 study of 165 participants [14][15][16]. A 2026 narrative review concluded that available data suggest treatment effects compared with placebo but that safety and efficacy need to be further characterized [2].

Early-phase studies. First-in-human work in healthy participants, along with studies of oral bioavailability under different gastric conditions, drug interactions, hepatic and renal impairment, and absorption, metabolism and excretion, have been published [11][12][13][17]. A report on its melanogenic effect has also appeared [18].
Systemic sclerosis. A phase 2 trial in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (76 participants) is registered as completed, supported by mouse-model data on skin fibrosis and lung inflammation [19].
Cosmetic use. No studies found of dersimelagon for cosmetic tanning, skin tone or other appearance outcomes.

Dersimelagon is a selective MC1R agonist that increases levels of skin eumelanin [6]. Unlike afamelanotide and other alpha-MSH analogues, it is not a peptide, and its discovery was reported in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry as a potent, selective, orally available agonist [10]. Reviews note that afamelanotide does not address the underlying disease mechanism of EPP, and that investigational agents such as dersimelagon and bitopertin are being studied partly because the approved drug is licensed only for adults [2]. MC1R signalling is one of five melanocortin receptor pathways linked with pigmentation, inflammation and other functions [4][5].

A review of EPP trial protocols examined new pharmacotherapies from the patient perspective, and a separate paper discussed whether placebo controls in EPP trials are ethical, given that photoprotection is not otherwise available to many patients [20][7]. Interest outside protoporphyria centres on MC1R's anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects [9][10].

timeline.event: Phase 3 trial of MT-7117 in EPP and XLP begins [14].
Phase 3 extension study and phase 2 trial in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis begin [15][19].
Phase 2 results in EPP and XLP published in the New England Journal of Medicine [6].
A further phase 3 study in EPP and XLP begins [16].
